result: Grid cells and place cells exhibit theta sequences during locomotion and replays during quiescence/sleep. These are well-established phenomena in the hippocampal formation and medial entorhinal cortex.
evaluation: Claims C1-C27 describe established experimental observations about grid cells, place cells, theta sequences, and replays. These are supported by extensive citations to experimental literature (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky 1971, Hafting et al. 2005, Skaggs et al. 1996, O'Neill et al. 2017, Lee and Wilson 2002, Foster and Wilson 2006, etc.) and represent well-accepted knowledge in the field.

result: Theta sequences and replay are hypothesized to facilitate cognitive functions like memory consolidation and planning, but their underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C28-C29 accurately describe the current state of knowledge: these phenomena are believed to be functionally important based on experimental evidence (Foster 2017, Ólafsdóttir et al. 2018, Zielinski et al. 2018), but the mechanistic basis is not fully understood. This provides motivation for the modeling work.

result: The continuous attractor network model for grid cell formation has been accumulating experimental support and posits specific local, symmetric synaptic configurations within the MEC.
evaluation: Claims C8, C30-C31 describe the continuous attractor model framework with appropriate citations to both theoretical work (Burak and Fiete 2009, Widloski and Fiete 2014) and experimental support (Couey et al. 2013, Yoon et al. 2013, Heys et al. 2014, Dunn et al. 2015, Fuchs et al. 2016, Zutshi et al. 2018, Gu et al. 2018). This establishes the foundation for the modeling approach.

result: The continuous attractor network architecture naturally produces theta sequences and replay as distinct consequences of modulating external input, while maintaining the ability to generate 2D grid cells through path integration.
evaluation: Claims C9, C32-C33, C168, C174 represent the central finding of the manuscript. The model simulations demonstrate that the same network architecture can produce both theta sequences (during runs with theta-modulated inhibition) and replays (during idle periods with reduced drive), as shown in Figures 1-8 and Videos. The model successfully generates grid cells (Figure 1) while also producing the sequential phenomena.

result: Driving inhibitory interneurons at theta frequency causes attractor bumps to oscillate in speed and size, giving rise to theta sequences and phase precession, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C104-C105, C109-C110, C169 describe the mechanistic basis for theta phenomena in the model. Figure 4A-B shows that inhibitory drive modulates bump size, Figure 4C demonstrates the conceptual mechanism for phase precession through bump size oscillations, and Figure 6A-B shows that inhibitory drive modulates bump speed. The model successfully reproduces phase precession (Figure 3) and theta sequences (Figure 5).

result: Decreasing input drive to all neurons produces traveling wavefronts of activity that are decoded as replays. These wavefronts are nucleated at attractor bumps and propagate through regions with subthreshold excitatory drive where inhibitory neurons remain silent.
evaluation: Claims C13, C140-C147, C172-C173 describe the mechanism for replay generation. Figure 7A shows the decreased drive during idle periods, Figure 7B shows the coexistence of attractor bumps (center) and wavefronts (edges), and Video 1 demonstrates wavefront nucleation and propagation. Figure 7C-D shows that these wavefronts are decoded as rapid trajectories (replays). The mechanistic explanation involving excitatory-to-excitatory connections and silent inhibitory neurons is consistent with the model architecture.

result: The model implements a fully spiking continuous attractor network with five overlapping populations (four excitatory, one inhibitory) on a 2D neural sheet. The network naturally develops a triangular lattice of activity bumps that move synchronously with animal motion, producing grid cells.
evaluation: Claims C37-C56 describe the model architecture and basic grid cell generation. Figure 1A shows the network architecture with connectivity patterns, Figure 1B shows the drive profiles, Figure 1C shows the self-organized triangular lattice of bumps, Figure 1D shows bump motion tracking animal trajectory, and Figure 1E shows resulting grid cell firing patterns. Table 1 provides complete parameter specifications. The model successfully generates grid cells as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

result: The grid pattern on the neural sheet drifts over time, introducing path-integration errors that are corrected by brief allocentric input representing border/boundary/landmark cells.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 describe the drift correction mechanism. The drift phenomenon is cited to prior work (Burak and Fiete 2009, Hardcastle et al. 2015), and the correction mechanism is motivated by experimental and theoretical work on allocentric cells (Ocko et al. 2018, Keinath et al. 2018, Evans et al. 2016, Raudies and Hasselmo 2015, Savelli et al. 2017). Figure 2A-B shows the implementation of allocentric corrections. This is a reasonable modeling choice to maintain stable representations.

result: Grid cells at different neural sheet locations correspond to different track positions. Recorded neurons exhibit either single or double firing fields depending on the orientation of the self-organized grid pattern, similar to experimental observations.
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 describe the recording and analysis approach. Figure 2C shows the correspondence between sheet location and track position, Figure 2D shows single-field examples, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 shows double-field examples. The comparison to O'Neill et al. 2017 (C67) is appropriate. The stochastic nature of grid orientation across simulations is a natural consequence of the self-organization process.

result: Grid cell activity is highest when inhibitory drive is lowest (theta troughs), consistent with experimental observations. Theta cycles are aligned to start at phase 0° at inhibitory drive troughs.
evaluation: Claims C68-C72 establish the correspondence between model dynamics and experimental LFP measurements. Figure 2E shows the relationship between inhibitory drive and multiunit activity. The alignment with experimental observations (Hafting et al. 2008, Buzsáki 2002, Feng et al. 2015) and the methodology of O'Neill et al. 2017 is appropriate and well-justified.

result: The model produces heterogeneous phase relationships with theta: phase-independent neurons (firing throughout the cycle), phase-locking neurons (preferring 360°), and phase-precessing neurons (decreasing phase with field progress), resembling MEC LIII and LII neurons.
evaluation: Claims C73-C77, C103 describe the diversity of phase behaviors. Figure 3A shows spike rasters, Figure 3B shows representative examples of each subgroup, and Figure 3F shows spike density plots for each subgroup. The model successfully reproduces the qualitative features of different neuron types observed experimentally (Hafting et al. 2008). The heterogeneity arises naturally from the model without requiring separate neuron types.

result: The model's circular-linear correlation magnitudes (0.17 ± 0.11) are lower than experiments (≈0.3-0.4), partly due to more phase-independent and phase-locking neurons. Circular-linear regression with a fit score cutoff of 0.4 and precession range cutoff of 60° distinguishes the three subgroups.
evaluation: Claims C78-C89 provide quantitative comparison with experiments. Figure 3C shows correlation magnitudes, Figure 3D shows fit scores, and Figure 3E shows regression slopes. The authors acknowledge the discrepancy with experiments (O'Neill et al. 2017) and provide a reasonable explanation: the model has more neurons with low correlation (phase-independent and phase-locking), which circular-linear correlation cannot distinguish (C82). The cutoff values are justified by comparison to experimental ranges (Ebbesen et al. 2016, Reifenstein et al. 2016).

result: Phase-precessing neurons show directional precession (negative slopes for rightward runs, positive for leftward), with preferred phase around 360° at field entry, matching experimental observations. Detailed features like the 75° decrease over 50% field progress also agree with experiments.
evaluation: Claims C90-C97 provide detailed comparison of phase precession properties. Figure 3E shows the directional bias in regression slopes, Figure 3F shows spike density plots with preferred phase at 360° and the detailed features mentioned. The comparison to Hafting et al. 2008 is appropriate. Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B shows robustness to cutoff choice. This represents strong agreement between model and experiment.

result: Phase precession statistics are independent of motion direction (omnidirectional), and precession range and correlation magnitude increase with animal speed, consistent with experimental observations.
evaluation: Claims C99-C102 describe additional phase precession properties. Figure 3—figure supplement 5E-F shows direction independence, and Figure 3—figure supplement 6A shows speed dependence with statistical significance (p = 0.002 and 0.0006). These findings match experimental reports (Climer et al. 2013, Jeewajee et al. 2014), providing further validation of the model.

result: Phase precession arises from bump size oscillations: neurons first spike when bumps are large (late phase), then at progressively smaller phases as the bump center approaches. Activity level determines phase behavior: high activity produces phase independence, low activity produces phase locking, and intermediate activity produces phase precession.
evaluation: Claims C106-C119 explain the mechanistic basis for phase precession. Figure 4C demonstrates the conceptual mechanism, Figure 4D shows average bump shapes at different phases, and Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 show how rescaling bump activity produces different phase behaviors. Figure 3—figure supplement 4D shows that firing rate correlates with phase behavior in the main model. The mechanism is supported by experimental observations (Jeewajee et al. 2014) linking spike counts to precession slopes.

result: Decoded position generally matches actual position but shows rapid forward sweeps (theta sequences) within each theta cycle. Theta sequences represent motion at 0.88 ± 0.15 m/s, approximately twice the actual speed of 0.50 ± 0.05 m/s, matching experimental observations.
evaluation: Claims C120-C125 describe theta sequence generation and properties. Figure 5A shows decoded position tracking actual position, Figure 5B shows the forward sweeps within theta cycles, and Figure 5C quantifies the speed ratio. The comparison to O'Neill et al. 2017 (≈1 m/s theta sequences vs ≈0.4-0.5 m/s actual speed) shows good quantitative agreement. Figure 5D illustrates the sequences relative to actual position.

result: Theta sequences arise from oscillations in bump speed: higher inhibitory drive produces faster bump motion. The 2× speed ratio is explained by bumps moving at maximal speed during theta peaks and not moving at troughs, with the average encoding actual speed. This mechanism is robust across different simulation configurations.
evaluation: Claims C126-C134 explain the mechanism for theta sequences. Figure 6A-B shows that inhibitory drive increases bump speed, Figure 6C-D shows the sawtooth pattern of peak activity location producing forward surges. The theoretical explanation for the 2× ratio (C133) is clear and testable. Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows robustness across parameters (speeds between 1.2-2.5× actual). This provides a mechanistic explanation for a previously unexplained experimental observation.

result: During slow wave sleep/quiescence, the neocortex is less active and the medial septum increases firing while losing oscillatory nature. The model represents these changes as decreased excitatory drive and decreased non-oscillating inhibitory drive.
evaluation: Claims C135-C138 describe the input changes during idle periods. The experimental basis is cited (Steriade et al. 2001, Simon et al. 2006), and Figure 7A shows the implementation. The authors acknowledge adapting findings from slow wave sleep to model quiescence, which is reasonable given the behavioral and electrophysiological similarities. This is a key manipulation that switches the network between operating regimes.

result: During idle periods, replays are generated as traveling wavefronts that traverse much of the track in ~100 ms at 7.0 ± 2.6 m/s (about 14× actual speed), matching experimental observations of 4-6 m/s. Replay count varies stochastically, but speed is characteristic and always much faster than theta sequences.
evaluation: Claims C139, C148-C154 describe replay properties. Figure 7B shows the coexistence of bumps and wavefronts, Figure 7C-D shows decoded replays, Figure 7E shows example replays with timing, Figure 7F shows count variability, and Figure 7G quantifies speed. The comparison to O'Neill et al. 2017 shows good agreement. Figure 7—figure supplement 4 shows parameter dependence. The explanation that wavefronts are fastest because they lack inhibition (C154) is mechanistically sound.

result: With lower velocity gain, there is clear correspondence between neural sheet location and track position. Replays nucleated at attractor bumps representing the current position tend to propagate away from it, producing a directional bias similar to hippocampal replay experiments.
evaluation: Claims C155-C162 describe replay directionality with lower velocity gain. Figure 8A shows the correspondence between sheet location and track position, Figure 8B shows the directional bias, and Figure 8C quantifies the difference between start and end positions. The comparison to hippocampal replay experiments (Diba and Buzsáki 2007, Davidson et al. 2009) is appropriate, though the authors note this hasn't been directly assessed for grid cells. This represents a testable prediction.

result: With periodic boundary conditions and uniform drive, the entire neural sheet exhibits attractor bumps during runs and wavefronts during idle periods, producing all essential phenomena. Allocentric input becomes essential as positional information completely disappears during idle periods.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 describe an alternative model configuration. Figure 8D-E shows the uniform drive, Figure 8F-G shows the resulting dynamics, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2-3 show that theta and replay phenomena are preserved. This demonstrates that the core mechanisms don't depend on the specific drive profile, though the need for allocentric input becomes more critical. This strengthens the generality of the findings.

result: Bump size and speed are not generally correlated across parameter changes, suggesting that phase precession and theta sequences could potentially exist independently under certain conditions.
evaluation: Claims C170-C171 describe the independence of the two theta-related mechanisms. Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows the lack of correlation between bump size and speed across parameter variations. The speculation that one phenomenon could exist without the other (C171) is reasonable given this independence, though it remains to be tested experimentally. This provides insight into the relationship between phase precession and theta sequences.

result: The model differs from previous continuous attractor models in three key ways: (1) fully spiking neurons capturing membrane potential reset, (2) excitatory-to-excitatory connections enabling wavefront propagation, and (3) varying external input between behavioral states. The network can instantly switch between theta and replay regimes without connectivity changes.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35, C175-C182 describe the key innovations of the model. The use of spiking neurons is documented in the methods and contrasted with rate-based models (Burak and Fiete 2009, Widloski and Fiete 2014). Excitatory-to-excitatory connections are motivated by recent experimental discoveries (Fuchs et al. 2016, Winterer et al. 2017, Schmidt et al. 2017, Zutshi et al. 2018). The input modulation is based on experimental observations (Steriade et al. 2001, Simon et al. 2006). These innovations enable the model to produce both theta and replay phenomena.

result: The model presents testable predictions: wavefronts could be observed by calcium imaging or analyzed in tetrode recordings. In 2D, wavefronts would represent a manifold of positions sweeping out a plane rather than a single trajectory, requiring new decoding techniques to distinguish.
evaluation: Claims C183-C187 describe experimental predictions and tests. The suggestions for calcium imaging (Heys et al. 2014, Diehl et al. 2019) and tetrode analysis are reasonable. The prediction about 2D wavefronts representing manifolds rather than trajectories (C186) is a logical extension of the model and represents a clear, testable prediction that distinguishes this mechanism from alternatives. The need for new decoding methods (C187) is appropriately acknowledged.

result: The same architecture that produces grid cells causes them to participate in sequences that may be leveraged by other brain regions like the hippocampus to pursue cognitive goals.
evaluation: Claim C36 is speculative about the functional role of these sequences in the broader hippocampal-entorhinal system. While the model demonstrates that sequences arise naturally from the grid cell architecture, the claim about how they are "leveraged" by other brain regions goes beyond what the model directly demonstrates. This represents a reasonable hypothesis but would require additional experimental evidence to support.
